question: In Sicily, the waste management situation of the landfill in the municipality of Mazzarà Sant’Andrea (Messina), which ceased operations in 2014, has become critical. Recently1, there have been some major fires in the area, causing so-called hidden fires below the landfill’s surface that continue to burn2.

The situation is compounded by the fact that charges have been brought by the Messina District Anti-Mafia Directorate for unlawful waste management, water poisoning, environmental pollution and environmental disaster, attesting to how devastating this has been for the environmental media (air, water, soil and subsoil) and how inadequately and dangerously the site has been managed3.

To this day, there are still major issues with how emergencies and urgent matters, such as the lack of effective waste coverage and the unsatisfactory leachate treatment system, are managed4. These shortcomings raise pressing concerns about compliance with Directive 1999/31/EC and Directive 2008/98/EC, which require Member States to take the necessary measures for the closure and after-care of landfills.
In view of the above: 1.
Is the Commission aware of the recent developments at the Mazzarà Sant’Andrea landfill? What specific action will it take to ensure compliance with EU legislation on waste management?
What support measures can it offer to ensure the clean-up and safety of the site, preventing further environmental damage and risks to public health?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (16.12.2024) 1. In line with its strategic approach on enforcement action1, the Commission aims to swiftly follow up on systemic cases. The Commission is currently pursuing two infringements cases against Italy for systemic non-compliance with EU law relating to illegal landfills.

Italy has been condemned to pay fines for 200 illegal landfills2 and for failure to ensure definite closure and rehabilitation of 44 landfills3. Individual cases such as the Mazzarrà landfill in Messina are better addressed at national level which can examine the situation on site, its surroundings and the characteristics of the waste deposited4.

Those authorities have to ensure that the provisions of the Landfill Directive5 are followed, including permitting, water control, leachate management, protection of soil and water, and procedures for closure and after-care6. 2.

The European Regional Development Fund (ERDF)7 can support Member States in interventions for rehabilitation of industrial sites and contaminated land, including investments for decommissioning, reconverting or making safe existing landfills provided that such investments do not increase their capacity, and in line with the polluters pay principle.

Priority is given by the Italian Partnership Agreement8 to interventions aimed at sites in the list of National and Regional Interest, with a clearly established timeframe and implementation capacity. For the case in Sicily, the ERDF Regional Programme includes an indicative allocation of around EUR 8.9 million for this type of interventions, on condition that they are included in the regional decontamination plan.
The choice of the specific initiative to support is under the responsibility of the regional authorities.
1 As set out in the Communication of 19 January 2017: EU law: Better results through better application -

C/2016/8600, OJ C 18, 19.1.2017, p. 10–20 and in the Communication of 13 October 2022: COM(2022) 518 final - Enforcing EU law for a Europe that delivers. 2 Case C-196/13: https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/en/TXT/?uri=CELEX:62013CJ0196.
